title: ASIC warns banks on wealth advice
full_text:
The corporate regulator has put the big four banks on notice over any return to wealth management for the masses, as federal Labor prepares to advance advice reforms following a lengthy delay.
Financial Services Minister Daniel Mulino is expected to recommit to long-awaited advice reform legislation when he speaks at the National Press Club later this month.
With details still being finalised, there is speculation in some quarters that Dr Mulino may progress some of the much-delayed Delivering Better Financial Outcomes (DBFO) reforms as part of a larger package to improve consumer protections in advice.
It comes in the wake of two investment scheme collapses that have shocked the financial services industry and cost 11,000 people their retirement savings.
DBFO was the government’s response to a 2022 review of the financial advice system that recommended ways to make advice fairer, simpler and more accessible.
It has been on the backburner since the collapses of the Shield Master Fund and First Guardian Master Fund, two schemes that took in $1bn of super savings from retail investors before they imploded.
In his speech on August 19, Dr Mulino is also expected to outline new rules that will shut down the high-pressure, cold-calling sales tactics used to drive retail investors into the two failed funds.
Without waiting for DBFO legislation to be pushed through, the nation’s biggest super fund, the $410bn AustralianSuper, this month registered a new entity, AustralianSuper Advice, as it prepares to offer more detailed advice to members.
But big super is still counting on the government following through with DBFO reforms that would allow funds to “nudge” or prompt members to seek financial advice, as well as clarity on what advice services can be charged across the whole membership base.
It comes as industry funds bleed members to retail platforms, as wealthier people shun big super for a more personalised advice-driven retirement journey.
Eyeing the nation’s swelling retirement honey pot, the major banks are also looking to push back into mainstream wealth management, with the bosses of ANZ and Westpac both signalling a desire to re-enter the retail advice market as they wait for DBFO reforms to move forward.
But as banks make noise on advice, Australian Securities & Investments Commission chair Sarah Court warned the sector to remember the lessons from the past.
“We understand the importance of access to good quality financial advice and support efforts that will enable Australians to get trusted financial advice more readily,” Ms Court told The Australian.
“We would want to ensure any re-entry into wealth management by banks is done in a way that has regard to the lessons from the financial services royal commission, particularly around potential harm around conflicts.
“Should banks return to this space, ASIC will be watching closely and monitoring customer complaints to ensure those lessons are not forgotten.
“ASIC would encourage banks to leverage technology, innovation and their own increased risk and compliance maturity in the design, implementation and ongoing monitoring of models, to ensure customer interests are put first.” The new ASIC chair’s comments come after ANZ chief executive Nuno Matos in recent months said banks should broaden their suite of offerings and get back into wealth management to boost their margins.
Similarly, Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller has warned that regulatory settings are holding banks back from providing even basic advice, such as being able to point customers to bank accounts with higher savings rates.
Association of Superannuation Funds of Australia chief executive Mary Delahunty urged the government to push ahead with the stalled DBFO reforms to lift access to financial advice.
“The sector needs clarity on the line between general and personal advice, on how they can use digital tools, and on how to discuss things like the Age Pension and transition-to-retirement strategies with their members,” Ms Delahunty said.
“These are things that members rightly expect their super fund can help them with as a trusted source of information.
“These are sorely needed reforms that will increase access to personalised advice. “What the government needs to do now is set out a clear pathway and timetable for these reforms, so the sector can get on with solving this problem.”
